overview: Machine Learning models do not learn fixed values — they learn uncertainty. Probability theory provides the language to describe uncertainty, starting with random variables and probability distributions.

This module covers random variables, common probability distributions, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, and the Law of Large Numbers — all essential foundations for understanding how ML models learn from data.

topics.title: Random Variables & Probability Distributions
theory: A random variable is a numerical outcome of a random process. It is not random itself — it maps randomness to numbers.

Discrete random variables take countable values (dice rolls, number of clicks, class labels). Continuous random variables take uncountably infinite values (height, time, loss values). Key distinction: Discrete uses probabilities, Continuous uses probability densities.

A probability distribution describes how likely different outcomes are. For discrete distributions, we use a Probability Mass Function (PMF) where P(X=x) gives exact probabilities. For continuous distributions, we use a Probability Density Function (PDF) where probability exists over ranges, not points.
Expected Value E[X] is the long-run average — the target most ML models optimize toward. Variance Var(X) measures uncertainty, risk, and model instability.
visualIntuition: Show randomness becoming structure: random points are generated appearing chaotic, then samples accumulate and a histogram shape emerges, finally a smooth distribution curve overlays the histogram showing randomness becoming order.
visualSuggestions: Button to add samples one by one, watching histogram emerge from chaos
Toggle between PMF (discrete bars) and PDF (continuous curve) for same underlying concept

from scipy.stats import bernoulli, norm

topics.title: Common Probability Distributions
theory: Bernoulli Distribution models a single binary trial: X ∈ {0, 1}, P(X=1) = p. Examples: click/no click, fraud/no fraud, pass/fail. Mean = p, Variance = p(1-p). In ML: Binary classification labels use Bernoulli, and cross-entropy loss is derived from Bernoulli likelihood.

Binomial Distribution models the number of successes in N independent Bernoulli trials: X ~ Binomial(n, p). Examples: number of users clicking an ad, defective items in a batch. Mean = np, Variance = np(1-p).

Normal Distribution is the most important continuous distribution: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Most values cluster around the mean; extreme values are rare but possible. Examples: measurement noise, model errors, aggregated natural processes. The Central Limit Theorem explains why it appears everywhere.

Central Limit Theorem: Regardless of the original distribution, the mean of samples converges to a normal distribution as sample size increases. This justifies using normal assumptions and explains why averages behave predictably.
visualIntuition: Distribution selector allowing users to switch between Bernoulli (single dot flipping), Binomial (histogram forming as trials increase), and Normal (bell curve). Parameter sliders for p, n, μ, σ to see distribution shapes change.
visualSuggestions: CLT demonstration: sample from skewed distribution, plot means, watch histogram become normal
Parameter sliders showing how mean and variance affect distribution shape

topics.title: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem
theory: Conditional probability answers: How likely is an event given that something else already happened? P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B). Conditional probability shrinks the universe — instead of asking how often A happens, you ask how often A happens inside the world where B is already true.

Independence vs Dependence: If P(A|B) = P(A), events are independent — knowing B tells you nothing about A. If P(A|B) ≠ P(A), events are dependent — B changes your belief about A. Machine Learning assumes dependence; if features were independent of labels, learning would be impossible.

Bayes' Theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). P(A) is the prior belief, P(B|A) is the likelihood, P(B) is the evidence, and P(A|B) is the posterior (updated belief). Bayes' theorem is belief updating: start with a belief, see evidence, update belief.

In ML: Bayes explains why models output probabilities, why predictions change with new data, why uncertainty matters. Applications include spam filtering, medical diagnosis, recommendation systems, and Naive Bayes classifiers.
visualIntuition: Belief updating visualization: Prior probability bar, evidence arrives and likelihood is applied, posterior shifts. Users see belief movement as parameters change.
visualSuggestions: Venn diagram showing how conditioning shrinks the sample space
Interactive prior slider showing how posterior changes with different priors

code.content:
# Prior belief
P_disease = 0.01

# Test accuracy
P_positive_given_disease = 0.95
P_positive_given_no_disease = 0.05

# Evidence (total probability of positive test)
P_positive = (
    P_positive_given_disease * P_disease +
    P_positive_given_no_disease * (1 - P_disease)
)

# Posterior (Bayes' theorem)
P_disease_given_positive = (
    P_positive_given_disease * P_disease
) / P_positive

print(f"P(disease | positive test): {P_disease_given_positive:.4f}")
print("Key lesson: Even accurate tests produce low confidence if priors are low!")

topics.title: Poisson Distribution
theory: The Poisson distribution models the number of discrete events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, given that events happen at a known constant mean rate λ (lambda) and independently of each other.
PMF: P(X = k) = (λ^k · e^{-λ}) / k!
Key properties: Mean = λ, Variance = λ (unique: mean equals variance), Skewness = 1/√λ.
ML Use Cases: Count-based NLP models (word frequency), anomaly detection for rare events (network intrusions), recommendation systems (click/purchase counts), and queueing theory (server requests).
visualIntuition: Imagine counting how many emails you receive per hour. Some hours you get 0, some hours 5. The Poisson distribution describes this pattern — given an average rate λ, it tells you the probability of any specific count.
visualSuggestions: Interactive PMF bar chart with λ slider — watch distribution shape shift from right-skewed to symmetric
Sample generator: click to add random events, histogram builds toward theoretical PMF

code.description: Poisson Distribution - PMF, CDF, and Visualization
code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create Poisson distribution with lambda=4
rv = stats.poisson(mu=4)

# PMF: probability of exactly k=3 events
print(rv.pmf(3))         # 0.1954

# CDF: probability of k <= 5 events
print(rv.cdf(5))         # 0.7851

# Descriptive statistics
print(rv.mean())         # 4.0
print(rv.var())          # 4.0  (always equals lambda)
print(rv.std())          # 2.0

# Generate random samples
samples = rv.rvs(size=1000, random_state=42)
print(np.mean(samples))  # ~= 4.0

# Plot PMF
k = np.arange(0, 15)
plt.bar(k, rv.pmf(k), color='steelblue', alpha=0.7)
plt.xlabel('k (events)')
plt.ylabel('P(X=k)')
plt.title('Poisson PMF (lambda=4)')
plt.show()

topics.title: Exponential Distribution
theory: The Exponential distribution models the time between consecutive events in a Poisson process. It is the continuous counterpart to the Poisson distribution.
PDF: f(x) = λ · e^{-λx} for x ≥ 0
Key property — Memorylessness: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). The probability of waiting an additional time t is the same regardless of how long you've already waited.
ML Use Cases: Survival analysis and customer churn modelling, time-to-failure predictions in reliability engineering, fraud detection (inter-transaction times).
visualIntuition: Imagine waiting for a bus that arrives randomly. The Exponential distribution tells you the probability of waiting a certain amount of time. Its memoryless property means that if you've already waited 10 minutes, the expected additional wait is still the same.
visualSuggestions: PDF curve with λ slider — heavier tail (slower decay) for smaller λ
Memorylessness demo: progress bar resets, showing waiting time is independent of elapsed time

code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

# Exponential with rate=0.5 (mean = 1/0.5 = 2)
rv = stats.expon(scale=2)  # scipy uses scale = 1/rate

# Mean and std
print(rv.mean())           # 2.0
print(rv.std())            # 2.0  (always equals mean)

# Memorylessness verification
# P(X > 5 | X > 3) should equal P(X > 2)
print(rv.sf(5) / rv.sf(3)) # ~= 0.3679
print(rv.sf(2))            # ~= 0.3679  - they match!

topics.title: Uniform Distribution
theory: The Uniform distribution assigns equal probability to all outcomes in an interval [a, b]. Every value is equally likely.
PDF: f(x) = 1/(b-a) for a ≤ x ≤ b, else 0
Key properties: Mean = (a+b)/2, Variance = (b-a)²/12, Entropy is maximised among all distributions with the same support.
ML Use Cases: Weight initialisation in neural networks, hyperparameter search limits, data augmentation.
visualIntuition: Think of a perfectly fair spinner on a circular dial. No matter where the needle lands between a and b, every position is equally likely. The probability is simply 1/(b-a) everywhere in the interval.
visualSuggestions: Flat PDF rectangle with [a,b] sliders — CDF shows linear ramp
Inverse transform sampling demo: uniform draws on y-axis mapped through CDF inverse to target distribution

from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

# Uniform between 2 and 8 (loc=a, scale=b-a)
rv = stats.uniform(loc=2, scale=6)

# PDF (constant within range)
print(rv.pdf(5))           # 0.1667 (= 1/6)

# Neural network weight initialisation
def uniform_init(shape, a=-0.1, b=0.1):
    return np.random.uniform(a, b, shape)

W = uniform_init((128, 64))
print(W.min(), W.max())    # ~= -0.1, 0.1

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a PMF and a PDF?
options: PMF is for continuous, PDF for discrete
PMF gives exact probabilities, PDF gives densities over ranges
PMF uses integrals, PDF uses sums
They are the same thing
quiz.explanation: A PMF (Probability Mass Function) assigns exact probabilities to discrete outcomes like P(X=3). A PDF (Probability Density Function) describes continuous distributions where probability exists only over ranges, not individual points.

quiz.question: Why does cross-entropy loss relate to the Bernoulli distribution?
options: Both use normal distributions
Cross-entropy measures the log-likelihood of Bernoulli outcomes
They share the same variance formula
Cross-entropy only works with continuous data
quiz.explanation: Binary classification labels follow a Bernoulli distribution (0 or 1). Cross-entropy loss is derived from the negative log-likelihood of this Bernoulli model, measuring how well predicted probabilities match actual binary outcomes.

quiz.question: Given P(disease)=0.01 and a test with 95% sensitivity and 5% false positive rate, what is approximately P(disease|positive)?
quiz.explanation: Using Bayes' theorem: P(D|+) = (0.95 × 0.01) / (0.95×0.01 + 0.05×0.99) ≈ 0.16 or 16%. Even with an accurate test, rare conditions produce surprisingly low posterior probabilities.

quiz.question: Why does the Law of Large Numbers matter for training ML models?
options: It guarantees perfect predictions
Sample statistics converge to true parameters with more data
It eliminates all bias
It only applies to normal distributions
quiz.explanation: LLN ensures that as training data grows, sample statistics (means, variances) converge to true population parameters. This is why models improve with more data and why validation metrics stabilize.

quiz.question: What does it mean for two events to be independent?
options: They never occur together
P(A|B) = P(A) — knowing B tells you nothing about A
They have the same probability
They are mutually exclusive
quiz.explanation: Independence means P(A|B) = P(A). Knowing that B occurred doesn't change your belief about A. This is different from mutual exclusivity, where events cannot co-occur.

quiz.question: What unique property does the Poisson distribution have regarding its mean and variance?
options: Mean is always twice the variance
Mean equals the variance
Variance is always zero
Mean is always greater than variance
quiz.explanation: For a Poisson distribution with parameter λ, both the mean and variance equal λ. This is a unique identifying property.

quiz.question: What does the memorylessness property of the Exponential distribution mean?
options: The distribution has no parameters to remember
Past waiting time does not affect future waiting probability
The distribution forgets its mean after each sample
Samples are always independent
quiz.explanation: Memorylessness means P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t). If you've already waited s units, the probability of waiting an additional t units is the same as starting fresh.

quiz.question: Which ML application commonly uses the Uniform distribution?
options: Computing loss functions
Neural network weight initialisation
Gradient descent step size
Batch normalization
quiz.explanation: Uniform distribution is commonly used for neural network weight initialisation (e.g., Xavier uniform), where weights are sampled from a small symmetric interval around 0.
